{{Short description|Parabolic partial differential equation}}
{{Use mdy dates|date = March 2019}}
{{Use American English|date = March 2019}}

In the field of [[differential geometry]] in [[mathematics]], '''mean curvature flow''' is an example of a [[geometric flow]] of [[Glossary of differential geometry and topology#H|hypersurfaces]] in a [[Riemannian manifold]] (for example, smooth surfaces in 3-dimensional [[Euclidean space]]). Intuitively, a family of surfaces evolves under mean curvature flow if the normal component of the velocity of which a point on the surface moves is given by the [[mean curvature]] of the surface.  For example, a round [[sphere]] evolves under mean curvature flow by shrinking inward uniformly (since the mean curvature vector of a sphere points inward).  Except in special cases, the mean curvature flow develops [[Mathematical singularity|singularities]].

Under the constraint that volume enclosed is constant, this is called [[surface tension]] flow.

It is a [[parabolic partial differential equation]], and can be interpreted as "smoothing".

==Existence and uniqueness==
The following was shown by [[Michael Gage (mathematician)|Michael Gage]] and [[Richard S. Hamilton]] as an application of Hamilton's general existence theorem for parabolic geometric flows.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gage |first1=M. |last2=Hamilton |first2=R.S. |title=The heat equation shrinking convex plane curves |journal=J. Differential Geom. |date=1986 |volume=23 |issue=1 |pages=69–96|doi=10.4310/jdg/1214439902 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hamilton |first1=Richard S. |title=Three-manifolds with positive Ricci curvature |journal=Journal of Differential Geometry |date=1982 |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=255–306|doi=10.4310/jdg/1214436922 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Let <math>M</math> be a compact [[Differentiable manifold|smooth manifold]], let <math>(M',g)</math> be a complete smooth [[Riemannian manifold]], and let <math>f:M\to M'</math> be a smooth [[Immersion (mathematics)|immersion]]. Then there is a positive number <math>T</math>, which could be infinite, and a map <math>F:[0,T)\times M\to M'</math> with the following properties:
* <math>F(0,\cdot)=f</math>
* <math>F(t,\cdot):M\to M'</math> is a smooth immersion for any <math>t\in[0,T)</math>
* as <math>t\searrow 0,</math> one has <math>F(t,\cdot)\to f</math> in <math>C^\infty</math>
* for any <math>(t_0,p)\in(0,T)\times M</math>, the derivative of the curve <math>t\mapsto F(t,p)</math> at <math>t_0</math> is equal to the [[mean curvature]] vector of <math>F(t_0,\cdot)</math> at <math>p</math>.
* if <math>\widetilde{F}:[0,\widetilde{T})\times M\to M'</math> is any other map with the four properties above, then <math>\widetilde{T}\leq T</math> and <math>\widetilde{F}(t,p)=F(t,p)</math> for any <math>(t,p)\in [0,\widetilde{T})\times M.</math>
Necessarily, the restriction of <math>F</math> to <math>(0,T)\times M</math> is <math>C^\infty</math>.

One refers to <math>F</math> as the (maximally extended) mean curvature flow with initial data <math>f</math>.

==Convex solutions==
Following Hamilton's epochal 1982 work on the [[Ricci flow]], in 1984 [[Gerhard Huisken]] employed the same methods for the mean curvature flow to produce the following analogous result:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Huisken |first1=Gerhard |title=Flow by mean curvature of convex surfaces into spheres |journal=J. Differential Geom. |date=1984 |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=237–266|doi=10.4310/jdg/1214438998 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* If <math>(M',g)</math> is the Euclidean space <math>\mathbb{R}^{n+1}</math>, where <math>n\geq 2</math> denotes the dimension of <math>M</math>, then <math>T</math> is necessarily finite. If the [[second fundamental form]] of the 'initial immersion' <math>f</math> is strictly positive, then the second fundamental form of the immersion <math>F(t,\cdot)</math> is also strictly positive for every <math>t\in(0,T)</math>, and furthermore if one choose the function <math>c:(0,T)\to(0,\infty)</math> such that the volume of the Riemannian manifold <math>(M,(c(t)F(t,\cdot))^\ast g_{\text{Euc}})</math> is independent of <math>t</math>, then as <math>t\nearrow T</math> the immersions <math>c(t)F(t,\cdot):M\to\mathbb{R}^{n+1}</math> smoothly converge to an immersion whose image in <math>\mathbb{R}^{n+1}</math> is a round sphere.
Note that if <math>n\geq 2</math> and <math>f:M\to\mathbb{R}^{n+1}</math> is a smooth hypersurface immersion whose second fundamental form is positive, then the [[Gauss map]] <math>\nu:M\to S^n</math> is a diffeomorphism, and so one knows from the start that <math>M</math> is diffeomorphic to <math>S^n</math> and, from elementary [[differential topology]], that all immersions considered above are embeddings.

Gage and Hamilton extended Huisken's result to the case <math>n=1</math>. Matthew Grayson (1987) showed that if <math>f:S^1\to\mathbb{R}^2</math> is any smooth embedding, then the mean curvature flow with initial data <math>f</math> eventually consists exclusively of embeddings with strictly positive curvature, at which point Gage and Hamilton's result applies.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Grayson |first1=Matthew A. |title=The heat equation shrinks embedded plane curves to round points |journal=J. Differential Geom. |date=1987 |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=285–314|doi=10.4310/jdg/1214441371 |doi-access=free }}</ref> In summary:
* If <math>f:S^1\to\mathbb{R}^2</math> is a smooth embedding, then consider the mean curvature flow <math>F:[0,T)\times S^1\to\mathbb{R}^2</math> with initial data <math>f</math>. Then <math>F(t,\cdot):S^1\to\mathbb{R}^2</math> is a smooth embedding for every <math>t\in(0,T)</math> and there exists <math>t_0\in(0,T)</math> such that <math>F(t,\cdot):S^1\to\mathbb{R}^2</math> has positive (extrinsic) curvature for every <math>t\in(t_0,T)</math>. If one selects the function <math>c</math> as in Huisken's result, then as <math>t\nearrow T</math> the embeddings <math>c(t)F(t,\cdot):S^1\to\mathbb{R}^2</math> converge smoothly to an embedding whose image is a round circle.

==Properties==
The mean curvature flow [[extremalization|extremalizes]] surface area, and [[minimal surface]]s are the critical points for the mean curvature flow; minima solve the [[isoperimetric]] problem.

For manifolds embedded in a [[Kähler–Einstein metric|Kähler–Einstein manifold]], if the surface is a [[Lagrangian submanifold]], the mean curvature flow is of Lagrangian type, so the surface evolves within the class of Lagrangian submanifolds.

[[Huisken's monotonicity formula]] gives a monotonicity property of the [[convolution]] of a time-reversed [[heat kernel]] with a surface undergoing the mean curvature flow.

Related flows are:
* [[Curve-shortening flow]], the one-dimensional case of mean curvature flow
* the surface tension flow
* the Lagrangian mean curvature flow
* the [[inverse mean curvature flow]]

==Mean curvature flow of a 2D surface==
For a 2D surface embedded in <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math> as <math>z=S(x,y)</math> , the differential equation for mean-curvature flow is given by

:<math>\frac{\partial S}{\partial t} = 2D\ H(x,y) \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial y}\right)^2}
</math>

with <math>D</math> being a constant relating the curvature and the speed of the surface normal, and
the mean curvature being

:<math>
\begin{align}
H(x,y) & = 
\frac{1}{2}\frac{
\left(1 + \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial x}\right)^2\right) \frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial y^2} - 
2 \frac{\partial S}{\partial x} \frac{\partial S}{\partial y} \frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial x \partial y} + 
\left(1 + \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial y}\right)^2\right) \frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial x^2}
}{\left(1 + \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial y}\right)^2\right)^{3/2}}.
\end{align}
</math>

In the limits <math> \left|\frac{\partial S}{\partial x}\right| \ll 1 </math> and <math> \left|\frac{\partial S}{\partial y}\right| \ll 1 </math>, so that the surface is nearly planar with its normal nearly
parallel to the z axis, this reduces to a [[diffusion equation]]

:<math>\frac{\partial S}{\partial t} = D\ \nabla^2 S
</math>

While the conventional diffusion equation is a linear parabolic partial differential equation and does not develop
singularities (when run forward in time), mean curvature flow may develop singularities because it is a nonlinear parabolic equation.  In general additional constraints need to be put on a surface to prevent singularities under 
mean curvature flows.

Every smooth convex surface collapses to a point under the mean-curvature flow, without other singularities, and converges to the shape of a sphere as it does so. For surfaces of dimension two or more this is a theorem of [[Gerhard Huisken]];<ref>{{citation
 | last = Huisken | first = Gerhard | authorlink = Gerhard Huisken
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Journal of Differential Geometry
 | mr = 1030675
 | pages = 285–299
 | title = Asymptotic behavior for singularities of the mean curvature flow
 | url = http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.jdg/1214444099
 | volume = 31
 | year = 1990| doi = 10.4310/jdg/1214444099 | hdl = 11858/00-001M-0000-0013-5CFD-5
 | hdl-access = free
 }}.</ref> for the one-dimensional [[curve-shortening flow]] it is the Gage–Hamilton–Grayson theorem. However, there exist embedded surfaces of two or more dimensions other than the sphere that stay self-similar as they contract to a point under the mean-curvature flow, including the [[Angenent torus]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Angenent | first = Sigurd B. | authorlink = Sigurd Angenent
 | contribution = Shrinking doughnuts
 | contribution-url = http://www.math.wisc.edu/~angenent/preprints/1989Gregynog/Gregynog.pdf
 | mr = 1167827
 | pages = 21–38
 | publisher = Birkhäuser | location = Boston, MA
 | series = Progress in Nonlinear Differential Equations and their Applications
 | title = Nonlinear diffusion equations and their equilibrium states, 3 (Gregynog, 1989)
 | volume = 7
 | year = 1992}}.</ref>

==Example: mean curvature flow of ''m''-dimensional spheres==
A simple example of mean curvature flow is given by a family of concentric round [[hypersphere]]s in <math>\mathbb{R}^{m+1}</math>. The mean curvature of an <math>m</math>-dimensional sphere of radius <math>R</math> is <math>H = m/R</math>.

Due to the [[rotational symmetry]] of the sphere (or in general, due to the invariance of mean curvature under [[isometry|isometries]]) the mean curvature flow equation <math>\partial_t F = - H \nu</math> reduces to the [[ordinary differential equation]], for an initial sphere of radius <math>R_0</math>,
:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}R(t) & = - \frac{m}{R(t)} , \\
R(0) & = R_0 .
\end{align}</math>

The solution of this ODE (obtained, e.g., by [[separation of variables]]) is 
:<math>R(t) = \sqrt{R_0^2 - 2 m t}</math>, 
which exists for <math>t \in (-\infty,R_0^2/2m)</math>.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Ecker | first = Klaus
 | doi = 10.1007/978-0-8176-8210-1
 | isbn = 0-8176-3243-3
 | location = Boston, MA
 | mr = 2024995
 | publisher = Birkhäuser
 | series = Progress in Nonlinear Differential Equations and their Applications
 | title = Regularity Theory for Mean Curvature Flow
 | volume = 57
 | year = 2004| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>
